entries.2ed9dfa4ab90c818590ae4f89d4130536092b1f2: <div sID="gen20660" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Zeph.2" sID="Zeph.2"/> <div eID="gen20660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20661" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20662" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. An earnest exhortation to the nation of the Jews to repent and make their peace with God, and so to prevent the judgments threatened before it was too late (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1-Zeph.2.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), and this inferred from the revelation of God's wrath against them in the foregoing chapter. II. A denunciation of the judgments of God against several of the neighbouring nations that had assisted, or rejoiced in, the calamity of Israel. 1. The Philistines, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.4-Zeph.2.7">ver. 4-7</reference>. 2. The Moabites and Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8-Zeph.2.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. 3. The Ethiopians and Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.12-Zeph.2.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. All these shall drink of the same cup of trembling that is put into the hands of God's people, as was also foretold by other prophets before and after.
entries.254896063fc944e12459f3e79082425d3e687555: <div eID="gen20662" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20661" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The People Exhorted to Repent. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20663" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired; <hi type="super">2</hi> Before the decree bring forth, <hi type="italic">before</hi> the day pass as the chaff, before the fierce anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> come upon you, before the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anger come upon you. <hi type="super">3</hi> Seek ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anger. <div eID="gen20663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> Here we see what the prophet meant in that terrible description of the approaching judgments which we had in the foregoing chapter. From first to last his design was, not to drive the people to despair, but to drive them to God and to their duty—not to frighten them out of their wits, but to frighten them out of their sins. In pursuance of that he here calls them to repentance, national repentance, as the only way to prevent national ruin. Observe, <div eID="gen20664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20665" type="x-p"/> I. The summons given them to a national assembly (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gather yourselves together.</hi> He had told them, in the last words of the foregoing chapter, that God would make a <hi type="italic">speedy riddance of all that dwelt in the land,</hi> upon which, one would think, it should follow, "Disperse yourselves, and flee for shelter where you can find a place." When the decree had absolutely gone forth for the last destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, that was the advice given (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">Matt. xxiv. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Then let those who are in Judea flee into the mountains;</hi> but here it is otherwise. God warns, that he may not wound, threatens, that he may not strike, and therefore calls to the people to use means for the turning away of his wrath. The summons is given to a <hi type="italic">nation not desired.</hi> The word signifies either, 1. <hi type="italic">Not desiring,</hi> that has not any desires towards God or the remembrance of his name, is not desirous of his favour or grace, but very indifferent to it, has no mind to repent and reform. "Yet <hi type="italic">come together,</hi> and see if you can stir up desires in one another." Thus God is often <hi type="italic">found of those that sought him not,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">asked for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa. lxv. 1</reference>. Or, 2. <hi type="italic">Not desirable,</hi> no ways lovely, nor having any thing in them amiable, or which might recommend them to God. The land of Israel had been a <hi type="italic">pleasant land, a land of delight</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">Dan. xi. 41</reference>); but now it is unlovely, it is a <hi type="italic">nation not desired,</hi> to which God might justly say, <hi type="italic">Depart from me;</hi> but he says, "<hi type="italic">Gather together to me,</hi> and let us see if any expedient can be found out for the preventing of the ruin. <hi type="italic">Gather together,</hi> that you may in a body humble yourselves before God, may fast, and pray, and seek his face. <hi type="italic">Gather together,</hi> to consult among yourselves what is to be done in this critical juncture, that every one may consider of it, may give and take advice, and speak his mind, and that what is done may be done by consent and so may be a national act." Some read it, "<hi type="italic">Enquire into yourselves,</hi> yea, <hi type="italic">enquire into yourselves;</hi> examine your consciences; look into your hearts; search and try your ways; <hi type="italic">enquire into yourselves,</hi> that you may find out the sin by which God has been provoked to this displeasure against you, and may find out the way of returning to him." Note, When God is contending with us it concerns us to enquire into ourselves. <div eID="gen20665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20666" type="x-p"/> II. Arguments urged to press them to the utmost seriousness and expedition herein (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.2">v. 2</reference>): "Do it in earnest; do it with all speed before it is too late, <hi type="italic">before the decree bring forth, before the day pass.</hi>" The manner of speaking here is very lively and awakening, designed to make them apprehensive, as all sinners are concerned to be, 1. That their danger is very great, that their all lies at stake, that it is a matter of life and death, which therefore well requires and well deserves the closest application of mind that can be. It is not a trifle, and therefore is not a thing to be trifled about. It is the <hi type="italic">fierce anger of the Lord</hi> that is kindled against them, and is just ready to kindle upon them, that <hi type="italic">devouring fire</hi> which none can <hi type="italic">dwell with,</hi> which none can make head against or hold up their head under. "It is the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord's anger,</hi> the day set for the pouring out of the full vials of it, that you are threatened with, that <hi type="italic">great day of the Lord</hi>" spoken of, <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.14">ch. i. 14</reference>. "Are you not concerned to prepare for that day?" 2. That it is very imminent: "Bestir yourselves now quickly, <hi type="italic">before the decree bring forth,</hi> and then it will be too late, the opportunity will be lost and never retrieved. The decree is as it were big with child, and it will <hi type="italic">bring forth the day,</hi> the terrible day, which shall <hi type="italic">pass as chaff,</hi> which shall hurry you away into captivity as chaff before the wind." <hi type="italic">We know not what a day may bring forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Prov. xxvii. 1</reference>), but we do know what the decree will bring forth against impenitent sinners, whom therefore it highly concerns to repent in time, in <hi type="italic">the accepted time.</hi> Note, It is the wisdom of those whom God has a controversy with to agree with him quickly, while they are in the way, before his fierce anger comes upon them, not to be turned away. In a case of this nature delays are highly dangerous and may be fatal; they will be so if by them the heart is hardened. How solicitous should we all be to make our peace with God before the Spirit withdraw from us, or cease to strive with us, before the day of grace be over or the day of life, before our everlasting state shall be determined on the other side of the great gulf fixed! <div eID="gen20666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20667" type="x-p"/> III. Directions prescribed for the doing of this effectually. It is not enough to gather together in a consternation, but they must seriously and calmly apply to the duty of the day (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Seek you the Lord.</hi> That they might find mercy with God, they are here put upon seeking; for so is the rule—<hi type="italic">Seek, and you shall find.</hi> A general call was given to the whole nation to <hi type="italic">gather together,</hi> but little good is to be expected from the far greater part of them; if the land be saved, it must be by the interest and intercession of the pious few, and therefore to them the exhortation here is particularly directed. And observe, 1. How they are described—they are <hi type="italic">the meek of the earth,</hi> or of <hi type="italic">the land.</hi> It is the distinguishing character of the people of God that they are the <hi type="italic">meek ones of the earth;</hi> this is their badge; it is their livery. They are modest, and humble, and low in their own eyes; they are mild, and gentle, and yielding to others, not soon angry, not very angry, not long angry; they are the <hi type="italic">quiet in the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.35.20">Ps. xxxv. 20</reference>. And they are subject and submissive to their God, to all his precepts and all his providences. Actuated by this principle and disposition, they have <hi type="italic">wrought his judgments,</hi> that is, have obeyed his laws, observed his institutions, have made conscience of their duty to him, and have laid out themselves for the advancement of his honour and interest in the world. 2. What they are required to do; they must <hi type="italic">seek,</hi> which denotes both a careful enquiry and a constant endeavour, that they may know and do their duty. (1.) They must <hi type="italic">seek the Lord,</hi> seek his favour and grace, address him upon all occasions, ask of him what they need, seek him early, seek him diligently, and continue seeking him. (2.) They must <hi type="italic">seek righteousness.</hi> "Seek to God for the performance of his promises to you, and see to it that you abound yet more in duty to him; seek for the righteousness of Christ to be imputed to you, for the graces of God's Spirit to be implanted in you; hunger and thirst after them." (3.) They must <hi type="italic">seek meekness.</hi> This is a grace they were so eminent for that they were denominated <hi type="italic">the meek of the land,</hi> and yet this they must <hi type="italic">seek.</hi> Note, Those that are ever so good must still strive to be better, those that have ever so much grace must be still praying and labouring for more. Nay, those that excel in any particular grace must still seek to excel yet more in that, because in that most assaults will be made upon them by their enemies, in that most is expected from them by their friends, and in that they are most apt to be themselves secure. <hi type="italic">Si dixisti, Sufficit, periisti—Say but, I am all that I ought to be, and you are undone.</hi> In the difficult trying times approaching, the meek will find exercise for all the meekness they have, and all little enough, and therefore should seek it earnestly, and pray that when God in his providence gives them occasion for it he would by his grace enable them to exercise it, <hi type="italic">to show all meekness to all men,</hi> in all instances, that, <hi type="italic">as the day is, so may the strength be.</hi> <div eID="gen20667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20668" type="x-p"/> IV. Encouragements given to take these directions: <hi type="italic">It may be, you shall be hid in the day of the Lord's anger.</hi> 1. "You particularly that are the <hi type="italic">meek of the earth.</hi> Though the day of the Lord's anger do come upon the land, yet you shall be safe, you shall be taken under special protection. <hi type="italic">Verily it shall be well with thy remnant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.15.11">Jer. xv. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy life will I give unto thee for a prey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.45.5">Jer. xlv. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will deliver thee in that day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.39.17">Jer. xxxix. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">It may be, you shall be hid;</hi> if any be hid, you shall." Good men cannot be sure of temporal preservation, for <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all,</hi> but they are most likely to be hid, and stand fairest for a distinguishing care of Providence. It is expressed thus doubtfully to try if they will trust the goodness of God's nature, though they have but the <hi type="italic">it may be</hi> of a promise, and to keep up in them a holy fear and watchfulness lest they should seem to come short, and should do any thing to throw themselves out of the divine protection. Note, those that hold fast their integrity, in times of common iniquity, have reason to hope that God will find out a hiding-place for them, where they shall be safe and easy, in times of common calamity. They shall be hid (as Luther says) <hi type="italic">aut in cœlo, aut sub cœlo—either in heaven or under heaven,</hi> either in the possession of heaven or under the protection of heaven. Or, 2. "You of this nation, though it be a <hi type="italic">nation not desired,</hi> yet, in the day of the Lord's anger with the neighbouring nations, when his judgments are abroad, <hi type="italic">you shall be hid;</hi> your land shall be preserved for the sake of those few meek ones that stand in the gap to <hi type="italic">turn away the wrath of God.</hi>" It concerns us all to make it sure to ourselves that we shall be hid in the great day of God's wrath; and, if we hide ourselves in the chambers of duty, God will hide us in chambers of safety, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Isa. xxvi. 20</reference>. If we prepare an ark, that shall be our hiding-place, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.1">Gen. vii. 1</reference>.
entries.024c18cb310989ac624028fe866f275ab6aa79ae: <div eID="gen20668" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Punishment of the Philistines. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20669" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> For Gaza shall be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation: they shall drive out Ashdod at the noon day, and Ekron shall be rooted up. <hi type="super">5</hi> Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites! the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> against you; O Canaan, the land of the Philistines, I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the sea coast shall be dwellings <hi type="italic">and</hi> cottages for shepherds, and folds for flocks. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the coast shall be for the remnant of the house of Judah; they shall feed thereupon: in the houses of Ashkelon shall they lie down in the evening: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God shall visit them, and turn away their captivity. <div eID="gen20669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20670" type="x-p"/> The prophet here comes to foretel what share the neighbouring nations should have in the destruction made upon those parts of the world by Nebuchadnezzar and his victorious Chaldees, as others of the prophets did at that time, which is designed, 1. To awaken the people of the Jews, by making them sensible how strong, how deep, how large, the inundation of calamities should be, that the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord,</hi> which was near, might appear the more dreadful, and they might thereby be quickened to prepare for it as for a general deluge. 2. To comfort them with this thought, that their case, though sad, should not be singular (<hi type="italic">Solamen miseris socios habuisse doloris</hi>—<hi type="italic">The wretched find it consolatory to have companions of their woe</hi>), and much more with this, that though God had seemed to be their enemy, and to fight against them, yet he was still so far their friend, and an enemy to their enemies, that he resented, and would revenge, the indignities done them. <div eID="gen20670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20671" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have the doom of the Philistines, who were near neighbours, and old enemies, to the people of Israel. Five lordships there were in that country; only four are here named—<hi type="italic">Gaza</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ashkelon, Ashdod</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ekron;</hi> Gath, the fifth, is not named, some think because it was now subject to Judah. They were the <hi type="italic">inhabitants of the sea-coasts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">v. 5</reference>), for their country lay upon the Great Sea. The <hi type="italic">nation of the Cherethites</hi> is here joined with them, which bordered upon them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1 Sam. xxx. 14</reference>) and fell with them, as is foretold also, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.16">Ezek. xxv. 16</reference>. The Philistines' land is here called Canaan, for it belonged to that country which God gave to his people Israel, and was inserted in the grant made to them, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Josh. xiii. 3</reference>. This land is yet to be possessed (<hi type="italic">five lords of the Philistines</hi>), so that they wrongfully kept Israel out of the possession of it (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.3">Judg. iii. 3</reference>), which is now remembered against them. For, though the rights of others may be long detained unjustly, the righteous God will at length avenge the wrong. <div eID="gen20671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20672" type="x-p"/> I. It is here foretold that the Philistines, the usurpers, shall be dispossessed and quite extirpated. In general, here is a woe to them (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">v. 5</reference>), which, coming from God, denotes all misery: <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord is against them</hi>—the word of the former prophets, which, though not yet accomplished, will be in its season, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">Isa. xiv. 31</reference>. This word, now by this prophet, is against them. Note, Those are really in a woeful condition that have the word of the Lord against them, for no word of his shall fall to the ground. Those that rebel against the precepts of God's word shall have the <hi type="italic">threatenings</hi> of the word against them. The effect will be no less than their destruction, 1. God himself will be the author of it: "<hi type="italic">I will even destroy thee,</hi> who can make good what I say and will." 2. It shall be a universal destruction; it shall extend itself to all parts of the land, both city and country: <hi type="italic">Gaza shall be forsaken,</hi> though now a populous city. It was foretold (<reference osisRef="Jer.47.6">Jer. xlvii. 6</reference>) that <hi type="italic">baldness</hi> should come upon Gaza; Alexander the Great razed that city, and we find (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.26">Acts viii. 26</reference>) that Gaza was a desert. <hi type="italic">Ashkelon</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">a desolation,</hi> a pattern of desolation. <hi type="italic">Ashdod shall be driven out at noon-day;</hi> in the extremity of the scorching heat they shall have no shade, no shelter to protect them; but then, when most incommoded by the weather, they shall be forced away into captivity, which will be an aggravating circumstance of it. <hi type="italic">Ekron</hi> likewise shall be <hi type="italic">rooted up,</hi> that had been long taking root. The land of the Philistines shall be dispeopled; there <hi type="italic">shall be no inhabitant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">v. 5</reference>. God made the earth <hi type="italic">to be inhabited</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">Isa. xlv. 18</reference>), otherwise he would have made it in vain; but, if men do not answer the end of their creation in serving God, it is just with God that the earth should not answer the end of its creation in serving them for a habitation; man's sin has sometimes subjected it to this vanity. 3. It shall be an utter destruction. The sea-coast, which used to be a harbour for ships and a habitation for merchants, shall now be deserted, and be only <hi type="italic">cottages for shepherds</hi> and <hi type="italic">folds for flocks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.6">v. 6</reference>), and then perhaps put to better use than when it was possessed by the lords of the Philistines. <div eID="gen20672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20673" type="x-p"/> II. It is here foretold that the house of Judah, the rightful owners, shall recover the possession of it, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.7">v. 7</reference>. The remnant of those that shall <hi type="italic">return out of captivity,</hi> when God visits them, shall be made to <hi type="italic">lie down</hi> in safety <hi type="italic">in the houses of Ashkelon,</hi> to lie down <hi type="italic">in the evening,</hi> when they are weary and sleepy. There <hi type="italic">they shall feed</hi> themselves and their flocks. Note, God will at length restore his people to their rights, though they may be long kept out from them.
entries.5d4f172075d79c81ebc4da215426e4eac1163fc4: <div eID="gen20673" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Punishment of Various Nations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> against their border. <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">as</hi> I live, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the breeding of nettles, and salt-pits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them. <hi type="super">10</hi> This shall they have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> against the people of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">will be</hi> terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall worship him, every one from his place, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the isles of the heathen. <div eID="gen20674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20675" type="x-p"/> The Moabites and Ammonites were both of the posterity of Lot; their countries joined, and, both adjoining to Israel, they are here put together in the prophecy against them. <div eID="gen20675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20676" type="x-p"/> I. They are both charged with the same crime, and that was reproaching and reviling the people of God and triumphing in their calamities (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have reproached my people;</hi> while God's people kept close to their duty it is probable that they reproached them for the singularities of their religion; and now that they had revolted from God, and fallen under his displeasure, they reproached them for that too. It has been the common lot of God's people in all ages to be reproached and reviled upon one account or other. Thus the old serpent spits his venom; and pride is at the bottom of it; it is in their pride that they have <hi type="italic">magnified themselves against the people of the Lord of hosts,</hi> thinking themselves as good as they, as great, and every way as happy. It is the <hi type="italic">comtempt of the proud</hi> that God's people are filled with, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Ps. cxxiii. 4</reference>. They have <hi type="italic">spoken big</hi> (so some read it, <hi type="italic">magna locuti sunt—they have spoken great things) against their border</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">v. 8</reference>), against those of them that bordered upon their country, whom upon all occasions they insulted, or against the property they claimed, which they disputed, or the protection they boasted of, which they ridiculed; they <hi type="italic">spoke big against the people of the Lord of hosts</hi> as a deserted abandoned people. <hi type="italic">Great swelling words of vanity</hi> are the genuine language of the church's enemies. "But <hi type="italic">I have heard them</hi>" (says God), "and will let you know that I have heard them. I have heard, and I will reckon for them," <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. And, if God hears the reproaches and revilings we are under, it is a good reason why we should be as a <hi type="italic">deaf man that hears not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14-Ps.38.15">Ps. xxxviii. 14, 15</reference>. Nay, God not only takes notice of, but interests himself in the reproaches cast on his people, because they are his; and it is certain that those who look with disdain upon the people of the Lord of hosts thereby dishonour the Lord of hosts himself. See this very thing charged on Moab and Ammon, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.3">Ezek. xxv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen20676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20677" type="x-p"/> II. They are both laid under the same doom. Associates in iniquity may expect to be such in desolation. See with what solemnity sentence is pronounced upon them, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.9">v. 9</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> the sovereign Lord of all, who has authority to pass this sentence and ability to execute it; it is <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> who is jealous for their honour; it is he that has said it, nay, he has sworn it, <hi type="italic">As I live, saith the Lord.</hi> The sentence is, 1. That the Moabites and Ammonites shall be quite destroyed; they <hi type="italic">shall be as Sodom and Gomorrah,</hi> the marks of whose ruins in the Dead Sea lay near adjoining to the countries of Moab and Ammon; they shall, though not by the same means (even fire from heaven), Yet almost in the same manner, be laid waste; not again to be inhabited, or not of a long time. The country shall produce nothing but <hi type="italic">nettles,</hi> instead of corn; and there shall be <hi type="italic">brine-pits,</hi> instead of the pleasant fountains of water with which the country had abounded. 2. That Israel shall be too hard for them, shall <hi type="italic">spoil them</hi> of their goods and <hi type="italic">possess</hi> their country by lawful war. Note, Proud men sometimes, by the just judgment of God, fall under the mortification of being trampled upon themselves by those whom once they haughtily trampled upon. And <hi type="italic">this shall they have for their pride.</hi> <div eID="gen20677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20678" type="x-p"/> III. Other nations shall in like manner be humbled, that the Lord alone may be exalted (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord will be terrible</hi> unto the Moabites and Ammonites in particular, who have made themselves a terror to his Israel. For, 1. Heathen gods must be abolished. They have long had possession, and their worshippers have both glorified them and gloried in them. But <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> will <hi type="italic">famish all the gods of the earth,</hi> will starve them out of their strong-holds. The Pagans had a fond conceit that their idols were regaled by their offerings, and did <hi type="italic">eat the fat of their sacrifices,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.38">Deut. xxxii. 38</reference>. <hi type="italic">Omnia comesta à Belo—Bel has eaten all.</hi> But it is here promised that when the Christian religion is set up in the world men shall be turned from the service of these dumb idols, shall forsake their altars, and bring no more sacrifices to them, and thus they shall be famished, or <hi type="italic">made lean</hi> (as the word is), their priests shall. This intimates the vanity of those idols; it lies in the power of their worshippers to famish them; whereas the true God says, <hi type="italic">If I were hungry, I would not tell thee.</hi> It intimates also the victory of the God of Israel over them. <hi type="italic">Now know we that he is greater than all gods.</hi> 2. Heathen nations must be converted; when the gospel gets ground, by it men shall be brought to worship him who lives for ever (for that is the command of the everlasting gospel, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">every one from his place;</hi> they shall not need to go up to Jerusalem to worship the God of Israel, but wherever they are, they may have access to him. <hi type="italic">I will that men pray every where.</hi> God shall be worshipped, not only by all the tribes of Israel and the strangers who join themselves to them, but by all <hi type="italic">the isles of the heathen.</hi> This is a promise which looks favourably upon our native country, for it is one of the most considerable of the isles of the Gentiles, by which God will be glorified.
entries.bd77d0cceda76672cb8b8520dd3ec7a1feefb281: <div eID="gen20678" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ethiopia and Assyria Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 612.)</title> <div sID="gen20679" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Ye Ethiopians also, ye <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> slain by my sword. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he will stretch out his hand against the north, and destroy Assyria; and will make Nineveh a desolation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> dry like a wilderness. <hi type="super">14</hi> And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her, all the beasts of the nations: both the cormorant and the bittern shall lodge in the upper lintels of it; <hi type="italic">their</hi> voice shall sing in the windows; desolation <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in the thresholds: for he shall uncover the cedar work. <hi type="super">15</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I <hi type="italic">am,</hi> and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, <hi type="italic">and</hi> wag his hand. <div eID="gen20679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20680" type="x-p"/> The cup is <hi type="italic">going round,</hi> when Nebuchadnezzar is going on conquering and to conquer; and not only Israel's near neighbours, but those that lay more remote, must be reckoned with for the wrongs they have done to God's people; the Ethiopians and the Assyrians are here taken to task. 1. The Ethiopians, or Arabians, that had sometimes been a terror to Israel (as in Asa's time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.9">2 Chron. xiv. 9</reference>), must now be reckoned with: They <hi type="italic">shall be slain by my sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.12">v. 12</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar was God's sword, the instrument in his hand with which these and other enemies were subdued and punished, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. 2. The Assyrians, and Nineveh the head city of their monarchy, are next set to the bar, to receive their doom: <hi type="italic">He</hi> that is God's sword <hi type="italic">will stretch out his hand against the north, and destroy Assyria,</hi> and make himself master of it. Assyria had been the rod of God's anger against Israel, and now Babylon is the rod of God's anger against Assyria, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Isa. x. 5</reference>. He <hi type="italic">will make Nineveh a desolation,</hi> as was lately and largely foretold by the prophet Nahum. Observe, (1.) How flourishing Nineveh's state had formerly been (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly.</hi> Nineveh was so strong that she feared no evil, and therefore dwelt carelessly and set danger at defiance; she was so rich that she thought herself sure of all good, and therefore was a rejoicing city, full of mirth and gaiety; and she had such a dominion that she admitted no rival, but said in her heart, "<hi type="italic">I am, and there is none besides me</hi> that can compare with me, no city in the world that can pretend to be equal with me." God can with his judgments frighten the most secure, humble the most haughty, and mar the mirth of those that most laugh now. (2.) How complete Nineveh's ruin shall now be; it shall be made <hi type="italic">a desolation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.13">v. 13</reference>. Such a heap of ruins shall this once pompous city be that it shall be, [1.] A receptacle for beasts, such a wilderness that <hi type="italic">flocks shall lie down in it;</hi> nay, such a waste, desolate, frightful place, that wild beasts, shall take up their abode there; the melancholy birds, as the <hi type="italic">cormorant and bittern,</hi> shall make their nests in what remains of the houses, as they sometimes do in old ruinous buildings that are uninhabited and unfrequented. The <hi type="italic">lintels,</hi> or chapiters of the pillars, the <hi type="italic">windows</hi> and <hi type="italic">thresholds,</hi> and all the fine <hi type="italic">cedar-work</hi> curiously engraven, shall lie exposed; and on them these rueful ominous birds shall perch, and their <hi type="italic">voice shall sing.</hi> How are the songs of mirth turned into hideous horrid noises! What little reason have men to be proud of stately buildings, and rich furniture, when they know not what all the pomp of them may come to at last! [2.] A derision to travellers. Those that had come from far, to gratify their curiosity with the sight of Nineveh's splendour, shall now look on her with as much contempt as ever they looked upon her with admiration (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Every one that passes by shall hiss</hi> at her, and <hi type="italic">wag his hand,</hi> making light of her desolations, nay, and making sport with them—"There is an end of proud Nineveh." They shall not weep, and wring their hands (the adversities of those are unpitied and unlamented who were insolent and haughty in their prosperity), but they shall <hi type="italic">hiss and wag their hands,</hi> forgetting that perhaps their own ruin is not far off.  <chapter eID="Zeph.2"/> <div eID="gen20680" type="x-p"/>

entries.27f4379aa1e8fc0d5084d698787c2fa41b2ec7e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12940"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1-Zeph.2.15">Zep 2:1-15</reference>. Exhortation to Repent before the Chaldean Invaders Come. Doom of Judah's Foes, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, with Their Idols, and Ethiopia and Assyria.</title> <div sID="gen24221" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12940"/><hi type="bold">1. Gather yourselves--</hi>to a religious assembly, to avert the judgment by prayers (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.16">Joe 2:16</reference>) [Grotius]. Or, so as not to be dissipated "as chaff" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.2">Zep 2:2</reference>). The Hebrew is akin to a root meaning "chaff." Self-confidence and corrupt desires are the dissipation from which they are exhorted to gather themselves [Calvin]. The foe otherwise, like the wind, will scatter you "as the chaff." Repentance is the gathering of themselves meant.<div eID="gen24221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nation not desired--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.20">2Ch 21:20</reference>), that is, not desirable; unworthy of the grace or favor of God; and yet God so magnifies that grace as to be still solicitous for their safety, though they had destroyed themselves and forfeited all claims on His grace [Calvin]. The Margin from Chaldee Version has, "not desirous," namely of returning to God. Maurer and Gesenius translate, "Not waxing pale," that is, dead to shame. English Version is best. <div eID="gen24222" type="x-p"/>
entries.f330184a717ccdbb473dc7ea8f64ee3e9b5e9411: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12941"/><div sID="gen24223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12941"/><hi type="bold">2. Before the decree bring forth--</hi>that is, Before God's decree against you announced by me (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.1-Zeph.1.18">Zep 1:1-18</reference>) have its fulfilment. As the embryo lies hid in the womb, and then emerges to light in its own due time, so though God for a time hides His vengeance, yet He brings it forth at the proper season.<div eID="gen24223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before the day pass as the chaff--</hi>that is, before the day for repentance pass, and with it you, the ungodly, pass away as the chaff (<reference osisRef="Job.21.18">Job 21:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>). Maurer puts it parenthetically, "the day (that is, time) passes as the chaff (that is, most quickly)." Calvin, "before the decree bring forth" (the predicted vengeance), (then) the chaff (the Jews) shall pass in a day, that is, in a moment, though they thought that it would be long before they could be overthrown. English Version is best; the latter clause being explanatory of the former, and so the before being understood, not expressed. <div eID="gen24224" type="x-p"/>
entries.05ee6c4a0e09aa7ae0abc918b02282548efa21be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12942"/><div sID="gen24225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12942"/>3. As in <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1">Zep 2:1</reference> (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.12">Zep 1:12</reference>) he had warned the hardened among the people to humble themselves, so now he admonishes "the meek" to proceed in their right course, that so they may escape the general calamity (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.9">Psa 76:9</reference>). The meek bow themselves under God's chastisements to God's will, whereas the ungodly become only the more hardened by them.<div eID="gen24225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seek ye the Lord--</hi>in contrast to those that "sought not the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Zeph.1.6">Zep 1:6</reference>). The meek are not to regard what the multitudes do, but seek God at once.<div eID="gen24226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his judgment--</hi>that is, law. The true way of "seeking the Lord" is to "work judgment," not merely to be zealous about outward ordinances.<div eID="gen24227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek meekness--</hi>not perversely murmuring against God's dealings, but patiently submitting to them, and composedly waiting for deliverance.<div eID="gen24228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it may be ye shall be hid--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.6">Am 5:6</reference>). This phrase does not imply doubt of the deliverance of the godly, but expresses the difficulty of it, as well that the ungodly may see the certainty of their doom, as also that the faithful may value the more the grace of God in their case (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17-1Pet.4.19">1Pe 4:17-19</reference>) [Calvin]. Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.12">2Ki 25:12</reference>. <div eID="gen24229" type="x-p"/>
entries.538b232a74e352611057e2777bcff7bbc81c7836: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12943"/><div sID="gen24230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12943"/><hi type="bold">4. For--</hi>He makes the punishment awaiting the neighboring states an argument why the ungodly should repent (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1">Zep 2:1</reference>) and the godly persevere, namely, that so they may escape from the general calamity.<div eID="gen24230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gaza shall be forsaken--</hi>In the Hebrew there is a play of similar sounds, Gaza Gazubah; Gaza shall be forsaken, as its name implies. So the Hebrew of the next clause, Ekron teeakeer.<div eID="gen24231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the noonday--</hi>when on account of the heat Orientals usually sleep, and military operations are suspended (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5">2Sa 4:5</reference>). Hence an attack at noon implies one sudden and unexpected (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.4">Jr 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">15:8</reference>).<div eID="gen24232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ekron--</hi>Four cities of the Philistines are mentioned, whereas five was the normal number of their leading cities. Gath is omitted, being at this time under the Jews' dominion. David had subjugated it (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Ch 18:1</reference>). Under Joram the Philistines almost regained it (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Ch 21:16</reference>), but Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>) and Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.8">2Ki 18:8</reference>) having conquered them, it remained under the Jews. <reference osisRef="Amos.1.6">Am 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.5">Zec 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.20">Jr 25:20</reference>, similarly mention only four cities of the Philistines. <div eID="gen24233" type="x-p"/>
entries.53aa960938893e122a92554d6b12dab786bde703: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12944"/><div sID="gen24234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12944"/><hi type="bold">5. inhabitants of the seacoast--</hi>the Philistines dwelling on the strip of seacoast southwest of Canaan. Literally, the "cord" or "line" of sea (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.47.7">Jr 47:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.16">Eze 25:16</reference>).<div eID="gen24234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Cherethites--</hi>the Cretans, a name applied to the Philistines as sprung from Crete (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.23">De 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.47.4">Jr 47:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Am 9:7</reference>). Philistine means "an emigrant."<div eID="gen24235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Canaan ... land of the Philistines--</hi>They occupied the southwest of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.2">Jos 13:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">3</reference>); a name which hints that they are doomed to the same destruction as the early occupants of the land. <div eID="gen24236" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab392d283fa3d5c82a0f65dda3e7c8f12110d17b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12945"/><div sID="gen24237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12945"/><hi type="bold">6. dwellings and cottages for shepherds--</hi>rather, "dwellings with cisterns" (that is, water-tanks dug in the earth) for shepherds. Instead of a thick population and tillage, the region shall become a pasturage for nomad shepherds' flocks. The Hebrew for "dug cisterns," Ceroth, seems a play on sounds, alluding to their name Cherethites (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">Zep 2:5</reference>): Their land shall become what their national name implies, a land of cisterns. Maurer translates, "Feasts for shepherds' (flocks)," that is, one wide pasturage. <div eID="gen24237" type="x-p"/>
entries.8812850eec6d07718786298747bd471b240f8df8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12946"/><div sID="gen24238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12946"/><hi type="bold">7. remnant of ... Judah--</hi>those of the Jews who shall be left after the coming calamity, and who shall return from exile.<div eID="gen24238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed thereupon--</hi>namely, in the pastures of that seacoast region (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.6">Zep 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visit--</hi>in mercy (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.31">Ex 4:31</reference>). <div eID="gen24240" type="x-p"/>
entries.e55315290424cd0834a048c803c9b610ad4f640c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12947"/><div sID="gen24241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12947"/><hi type="bold">8. I have heard--</hi>A seasonable consolation to Judah when wantonly assailed by Moab and Ammon with impunity: God saith, "I have heard it all, though I might seem to men not to have observed it because I did not immediately inflict punishment."<div eID="gen24241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">magnified themselves--</hi>acted haughtily, invading the territory of Judah (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.29">Jr 48:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">49:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.10">Zep 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.26">Psa 35:26</reference>; Ob 12). <div eID="gen24242" type="x-p"/>
entries.81c6fc82681e53b0681e8f7f084b74728a9dc52c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12948"/><div sID="gen24243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12948"/><hi type="bold">9. the breeding of nettles--</hi>or, the overspreading of nettles, that is, a place overrun with them.<div eID="gen24243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salt pits--</hi>found at the south of the Dead Sea. The water overflows in the spring, and salt is left by the evaporation. Salt land is barren (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.45">Jud 9:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Psa 107:34</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen24244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">possess them--</hi>that is, their land; in retribution for their having occupied Judah's land. <div eID="gen24245" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ca59d04c256930a80edef063346af2ac5947ca9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12949"/><div sID="gen24246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12949"/>10. (Compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">Zep 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen24246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their pride--</hi>in antithesis to the meek (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.3">Zep 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen24247" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d3c100c78775be32223a178ffd9ad98ad5a5392: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12950"/><div sID="gen24248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12950"/><hi type="bold">11. famish--</hi>bring low by taking from the idols their former fame; as beasts are famished by their food being withheld. Also by destroying the kingdoms under the tutelage of idols (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.4">Psa 96:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Is 46:1</reference>).<div eID="gen24248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gods of the earth--</hi>who have their existence only on earth, not in heaven as the true God.<div eID="gen24249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one from his place--</hi>each in his own Gentile home, taught by the Jews in the true religion: not in Jerusalem alone shall men worship God, but everywhere (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Psa 68:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.30">30</reference>; Mal 1:11; <reference osisRef="John.4.21">Joh 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1Co 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Ti 2:8</reference>). It does not mean, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mi 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.22">Zec 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">14:16</reference> that they shall come from their several places to Jerusalem to worship [Maurer].<div eID="gen24250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... isles of ... heathen--</hi>that is, all the maritime regions, especially the west, now being fulfilled in the gathering in of the Gentiles to Messiah. <div eID="gen24251" type="x-p"/>
entries.d407ce7cd94d79eefa763f53ddc1f852d9dc6573: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12951"/><div sID="gen24252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12951"/>12. Fulfilled when Nebuchadnezzar (God's sword, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>) conquered Egypt, with which Ethiopia was closely connected as its ally (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.2-Jer.46.9">Jr 46:2-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5-Ezek.30.9">Eze 30:5-9</reference>).<div eID="gen24252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ye--</hi>literally, "They." The third person expresses estrangement; while doomed before God's tribunal in the second person, they are spoken of in the third as aliens from God. <div eID="gen24253" type="x-p"/>
entries.c025129c2d32335d45a0ff4869237870c7b54051: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12952"/><div sID="gen24254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12952"/>13. Here he passes suddenly to the north. Nineveh was destroyed by Cyaxares and Nabopolassar, 625 B.C. The Scythian hordes, by an inroad into Media and thence in the southwest of Asia (thought by many to be the forces described by Zephaniah, as the invaders of Judea, rather than the Chaldeans), for a while interrupted Cyaxares' operations; but he finally succeeded. Arbaces and Belesis previously subverted the Assyrian empire under Sardanapalus (that is, Pul?), 877 B.C. <div eID="gen24254" type="x-p"/>
entries.19c7db6a0693754171abde87a1075d1b99b03599: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12953"/><div sID="gen24255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12953"/><hi type="bold">14. flocks--</hi>of sheep; answering to "beasts" in the parallel clause. Wide pastures for sheep and haunts for wild beasts shall be where once there was a teeming population (compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.6">Zep 2:6</reference>). Maurer, needlessly for the parallelism, makes it "flocks of savage animals."<div eID="gen24255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beasts of the nations--</hi>that is, beasts of the earth (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.24">Ge 1:24</reference>). Not as Rosenmuller, "all kinds of beasts that form a nation," that is, gregarious beasts (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.25">Pr 30:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.26">26</reference>).<div eID="gen24256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cormorant--</hi>rather, the "pelican" (so <reference osisRef="Ps.102.6">Psa 102:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Is 34:11</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen24257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bittern--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.14.23">Is 14:23</reference>). Maurer translates, "the hedgehog"; Henderson, "the porcupine."<div eID="gen24258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upper lintels--</hi>rather, "the capitals of her columns," namely, in her temples and palaces [Maurer]. Or, "on the pomegranate-like knops at the tops of the houses" [Grotius].<div eID="gen24259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their voice shall sing in the windows--</hi>The desert-frequenting birds' "voice in the windows" implies desolation reigning in the upper parts of the palaces, answering to "desolation ... in the thresholds," that is, in the lower.<div eID="gen24260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall uncover the cedar work--</hi>laying the cedar wainscoting on the walls, and beams of the ceiling, bare to wind and rain, the roof being torn off, and the windows and doors broken through. All this is designed as a consolation to the Jews that they may bear their calamities patiently, knowing that God will avenge them. <div eID="gen24261" type="x-p"/>
entries.961c8b9e60ce548cfbc54fabe748bfe55d622803: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12954"/><div sID="gen24262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12954"/>15. Nothing then seemed more improbable than that the capital of so vast an empire, a city sixty miles in compass, with walls one hundred feet high, and so thick that three chariots could go abreast on them, and with fifteen hundred towers, should be so totally destroyed that its site is with difficulty discovered. Yet so it is, as the prophet foretold.<div eID="gen24262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there is none beside me--</hi>This peculiar phrase, expressing self-gratulation as if peerless, is plainly adopted from <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">Is 47:8</reference>. The later prophets, when the spirit of prophecy was on the verge of departing, leaned more on the predictions of their predecessors.<div eID="gen24263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hiss--</hi>in astonishment at a desolation so great and sudden (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1Ki 9:8</reference>); also in derision (<reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">La 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:36</reference>). <chapter eID="Zeph.2"/>

entries.d13e5e9fc105dc4715e96b3635f9a76f11f1bfa8: <div eID="gen35267" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35268" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35269" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35269" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35268" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35270" type="x-p"/> The prophet, having declared the judgments which were ready to fall on his people, earnestly exhorts them to repentance, that these judgments may be averted, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.1-Zep.2.3">Zep 2:1-3</reference>. He then foretells the fate of other neighboring and hostile nations: the Philistines, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.4-Zep.2.7">Zep 2:4-7</reference>; Moabites and Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.8-Zep.2.11">Zep 2:8-11</reference>; Ethiopians, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.12">Zep 2:12</reference>; and Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.13">Zep 2:13</reference>. In the close of the chapter we have a prophecy against Nineveh. These predictions were accomplished chiefly by the conquests of Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen35270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35271" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35272" type="x-p"/> Gather yourselves - Others, sift yourselves. Separate the chaff from the wheat, before the judgments of God fall upon you. O nation not desired - unlovely, not delighted in; hated because of your sin. The Israelites are addressed.
entries.0c2c9465a838650c87854a248650363f403ddb91: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35273" type="x-p"/> Ye meek of the earth - ענוי anavey, ye oppressed and humbled of the land. <div eID="gen35273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35274" type="x-p"/> It may be ye shall be hid - The sword has not a commission against you. Ask God, and he will be a refuge to you from the storm and from the tempest.
entries.838c56f8d32ff7e82ca43740a405e0e39e7c9e84: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35275" type="x-p"/> Gaza shall be forsaken - This prophecy is against the Philistines. They had been greatly harassed by the kings of Egypt; but were completely ruined by Nebuchadnezzar, who took all Phoenicia from the Egyptians; and about the time of his taking Tyre, devastated all the seignories of the Philistines. This ruin we have seen foretold by the other prophets, and have already remarked its exact fulfillment.
entries.2c1f9b2c444f0a4b5fb1bca0967591960550313c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35276" type="x-p"/> The sea-coasts, the nation of the Cherethites - The sea-coasts mean all the country lying on the Mediterranean coast from Egypt to Joppa and Gaza. The Cherethites - the Cretans who were probably a colony of the Phoenicians. See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sam 30:14</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Amo.9.7">Amo 9:7</reference> (note).
entries.86505b2ab81cb581fa16ed429c6463c2db07b888: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35277" type="x-p"/> And the sea-coasts shall be dwellings - Newcome considers כרת keroth as a proper name, not cottages or folds. The Septuagint have Κρητη, Crete, and so has the Syriac. Abp. Secker notes, Alibi non extat כרת, et forte notat patriam των כרתים. "The word כרת is not found elsewhere, and probably it is the name of the country of the Cherethim."
entries.f24f420cbb53c92f9d01a7563d64785cb4f8795e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35278" type="x-p"/> The coast shall be for the remnant - Several devastations fell on the Philistines. Gaza was ruined by the army of Alexander the Great, and the Maccabees finally accomplished all that was predicted by the prophets against this invariably wicked people. They lost their polity, and were at last obliged to receive circumcision.
entries.2040c74e6115c2c932b8d525cb11d29a293c8b5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35279" type="x-p"/> I have heard the reproach of Moab - God punished them for the cruel part they had taken in the persecutions of the Jews; for when they lay under the displeasure of God, these nations insulted them in the most provoking manner. See on <reference osisRef="Amo.1.13">Amo 1:13</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Gen.19.25">Gen 19:25</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Deu.29.23">Deu 29:23</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Isa 13:19</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Isa.34.13">Isa 34:13</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">Jer 49:18</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Jer.50.40">Jer 50:40</reference> (note).
entries.c0b414cbe90a5d5c1ba8782fedd15e2c9abe8c11: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35280" type="x-p"/> The breeding of nettles - That is, their land shall become desolate, and be a place for nettles, thorns, etc., to flourish in, for want of cultivation.
entries.be0b0f75428090d46b99dee37042df8ab5f2896a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35281" type="x-p"/> Because they have reproached - See on <reference osisRef="Zep.2.8">Zep 2:8</reference> (note).
entries.c15c276413d49003f6724781edf4d35f1aa62190: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35282" type="x-p"/> He will famish all the gods of the earth - They shall have no more sacrifices; their worship shall be entirely destroyed. Idolaters supposed that their gods actually fed on the fumes and spirituous exhalations that arose from the burnt-offerings which they made unto their idols. It is in reference to this opinion that the Lord says, "He will famish all the gods of the land."
entries.1173c78e377889a1fb0e61acb29241e94e7490aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35283" type="x-p"/> Ye Ethiopians also - Nebuchadnezzar subdued these. See <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.30.4">Eze 30:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.30.10">Eze 30:10</reference>. See also on <reference osisRef="Amo.9.7">Amo 9:7</reference> (note).
entries.b8f18e4783f34a47b032b553be47504d16536436: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen35283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35284" type="x-p"/> He will - destroy Assyria - He will overthrow the empire, and Nineveh, their metropolitan city. See on Jonah and Nahum.
entries.4639f141e8be530abcf8b2e7d3177fcbc926abaa: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen35284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35285" type="x-p"/> And flocks shall lie down in the midst of her - Nineveh was so completely destroyed, that its situation is not at present even known. The present city of Mossoul is supposed to be in the vicinity of the place where this ancient city stood. <div eID="gen35285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35286" type="x-p"/> The cormorant קאת kaath; and the bittern, קפד kippod. These Newcome translates, "The pelican and the porcupine." <div eID="gen35286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35287" type="x-p"/> Their voice shall sing in the windows - The windows shall be all demolished; wild fowl shall build their nests in them, and shall be seen coming from their sills, and the fine cedar ceilings shall be exposed to the weather, and by and by crumble to dust. See the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.34.11-Isa.34.14">Isa 34:11-14</reference> (note), where nearly the same terms are used. <div eID="gen35287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35288" type="x-p"/> I have in another place introduced a remarkable couplet quoted by Sir W. Jones from a Persian poet, which speaks of desolation in nearly the same terms. "The spider holds the veil in the palace of Caesar: <div eID="gen35288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35289" type="x-p"/> The owl stands sentinel in the watchtower of Afrasiab."
entries.08c89651fa3630927e1d4389e87568d06a39f5ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen35289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35290" type="x-p"/> This is the rejoicing city - The city in which mirth, jocularity, and pleasure, reigned without interruption. <div eID="gen35290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35291" type="x-p"/> And wag his hand - Will point her out as a mark and monument of Divine displeasure.  <chapter eID="Zeph.2"/> <div eID="gen35291" type="x-p"/>

entries.3ed668910559a22a9310e4aeb9b37a592283272e: Zep 2:1-3 <div eID="gen16717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16718" type="x-p"/> Call to conversion. - Zep 2:1. <hi type="italic">“Gather yourselves together, and gather together, O nation that dost not grow pale.</hi> Zep 2:2. <hi type="italic">Before the decree bring forth (the day passes away like chaff), before the burning wrath of Jehovah come upon you, before the day of Jehovah’s wrath come upon you.</hi> Zep 2:3. <hi type="italic">Seek Jehovah, all ye humble of the land, who have wrought His right; seek righteousness, seek humility, perhaps ye will be hidden in the day of Jehovah’s wrath.” </hi> The summons in Zep 2:1 is addressed to the whole of Judah or Israel. The verb <hi type="italic">qōshēsh</hi>, possibly a <hi type="italic">denom.</hi> from <hi type="italic">qash</hi>, signifies to gather stubble (<reference osisRef="Exod.5.7">Exo 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.5.12">Exo 5:12</reference>), then generally to gather together or collect, e.g., branches of wood (Num 15:32-33; 1Ki 17:10); in the <hi type="italic">hithpoel</hi>, to gather one’s self together, applied to that spiritual gathering which leads to self-examination, and is the first condition of conversion. The attempts of Ewald and Hitzig to prove, by means of doubtful etymological combinations from the Arabic, that the word possesses the meanings, to grow pale, or to purify one’s self, cannot be sustained. The <hi type="italic">kal</hi> is combined with the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> for the purpose of strengthening it, as in <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Hab 1:5</reference> and Isa 29:9. <hi type="italic">Nikhsâph</hi> is the perf. <hi type="italic">nipahl</hi> in pause, and not a participle, partly because of the לא which stands before it (see however Ewald, §286, <hi type="italic">g</hi>), and partly on account of the omission of the article; and <hi type="italic">nikhsâph</hi> is to be taken as a relative, “<hi type="italic">which</hi> does not turn pale.” <hi type="italic">Kâsaph</hi> has the meaning “to long,” both in the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.31.30">Gen 31:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.3">Psa 84:3</reference>) and <hi type="italic">kal</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.17.12">Psa 17:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.15">Job 14:15</reference>). This meaning is retained by many here. Thus Jerome renders it, “<hi type="italic">gens non amabilis</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">non desiderata a Deo</hi>;” but this is decidedly unsuitable. Others render it “not possessing strong desire,” and appeal to the paraphrase of the Chaldee, “a people not wishing to be converted to the law.” This is apparently the view upon which the Alex. version rests: ἔθνος ἀπαίδευτον. But although <hi type="italic">nikhsâph</hi> is used to denote the longing of the soul for fellowship with God in <reference osisRef="Ps.84.3">Psa 84:3</reference>, this idea is not to be found in the word itself, but simply in the object connected with it. We therefore prefer to follow Grotius, Gesenius, Ewald, and others, and take the word in its primary sense of turning pale at anything, becoming white with shame (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">Isa 29:22</reference>), which is favoured by Zep 3:15. The reason for the appeal is given in Zep 2:2, viz., the near approach of the judgment. The resolution brings forth, when that which is resolved upon is realized (for <hi type="italic">yâlad</hi> in this figurative sense, see <reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Pro 27:1</reference>). The figure is explained in the second hemistich. The next clause כּמוץ וגו does not depend upon בּטרם, for in that case the verb would stand at the head with <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> cop., but it is a parenthesis inserted to strengthen the admonition: the day comes like chaff, i.e., approaches with the greatest rapidity, like chaff driven by the wind: not “the time passes by like chaff” (Hitzig); for it cannot be shown that <hi type="italic">yōm</hi> was ever used for time in this sense. <hi type="italic">Yōm</hi> is the day of judgment mentioned in Zep 1:7, Zep 1:14-15; and עבר here is not to pass by, but to approach, to come near, as in Nah 3:19. For the figure of the chaff, see Isa 29:5. In the second בּטרם is strengthened by לא; and חרון אף, the burning of wrath in the last clause, is explained by יום אף יי, the day of the revelation of the wrath of God.
entries.b137334b19a5064fe780878408b7b4e3adc04120: Zep 2:4-5 <div eID="gen16719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16720" type="x-p"/> Destruction of the Philistines. - Zep 2:4. <hi type="italic">“For Gaza will be forgotten, and Ashkelon become a desert; Ashdod, they drive it out in broad day, and Ekron will be ploughed out.</hi> Zep 2:5. <hi type="italic">Woe upon the inhabitants of the tract by the sea, the nation of the Cretans! The word of Jehovah upon you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines! I destroy thee, so that not an inhabitant remains.</hi> Zep 2:6. <hi type="italic">And the tract by the sea becomes pastures for shepherds’ caves, and for folds of sheep.</hi> Zep 2:7. <hi type="italic">And a tract will be for the remnant of the house of Judah; upon them will they feed: in the houses of Ashkelon they encamp in the evening; for Jehovah their God will visit them, and turn their captivity.” </hi> The fourth verse, which is closely connected by <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> (for) with the exhortation to repentance, serves as an introduction to the threat of judgment commencing with <hi type="italic">hōi</hi> in Zep 2:5. As the mentioning of the names of the four Philistian capitals (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>) is simply an individualizing periphrasis for the Philistian territory and people, so the land and people of Philistia are mentioned primarily for the purpose of individualizing, as being the representatives of the heathen world by which Judah was surrounded; and it is not till afterwards, in the further development of the threat, that the enumeration of certain near and remote heathen nations is appended, to express more clearly the idea of the heathen world as a whole. Of the names of the Philistian cities Zephaniah makes use of two, <hi type="italic">‛Azzâh</hi> and <hi type="italic">‛Eqrōn</hi>, as a play upon words, to express by means of paronomasia the fate awaiting them. <hi type="italic">‛azzâh</hi>, Gaza, will be <hi type="italic">‛azûbhâh</hi>, forsaken, desolate. <hi type="italic">‛Eqrōn</hi>, Ekron, will be <hi type="italic">tē‛âqēr</hi>, rooted up, torn out of its soil, destroyed. To the other two he announces their fate in literal terms, the <hi type="italic">shemâmâh</hi> threatened against Ashkelon corresponding to the <hi type="italic">‛ăzūbhâh</hi>, and the <hi type="italic">gârēsh</hi> predicated of Ashdod preparing the way for Ekron’s <hi type="italic">tē‛âqēr</hi>. בּצּהרים at noon, i.e., in broad day, might signify, when used as an antithesis to night, “with open violence” (Jerome, Kimchi); but inasmuch as the expulsion of inhabitants is not effected by thieves in the night, the time of noon is more probably to be understood, as v. Cölln and Rosenmüller suppose, as denoting the time of day at which men generally rest in hot countries (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.5">2Sa 4:5</reference>), in the sense of unexpected, unsuspected expulsion; and this is favoured by <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jer 15:8</reference>, where the devastation at noon is described as a sudden invasion. The omission of Gath may be explained in the same manner as in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.6-Amos.1.8">Amo 1:6-8</reference>, from the fact that the parallelism of the clauses only allowed the names of four cities to be given; and this number was amply sufficient to individualize the whole, just as Zephaniah, when enumerating the heathen nations, restricts the number to four, according to the four quarters of the globe: viz., the Philistines in the west (Zep 2:5-7); the Moabites and Ammonites comprised in one in the east (Zep 2:8-10); the Cushites in the south (Zep 2:11, Zep 2:12); and Asshur, with Nineveh, in the north (north-east), (Zep 2:13-15). The woe with which the threat is commenced in Zep 2:5 applies to the whole land and people of the Philistines. <hi type="italic">Chebhel</hi>, the measure, then the tract of land measured out or apportioned (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deu 32:9</reference>, etc.). The tract of the sea is the tract of land by the Mediterranean Sea which was occupied by the Philistines (<hi type="italic">chebhel hayyâm</hi> = <hi type="italic">'erets Pelishtı̄m</hi>). Zephaniah calls the inhabitants <hi type="italic">gōi Kerēthı̄m</hi>, nation of the Cretans, from the name of one branch of the Philistian people which was settled in the south-west of Philistia, for the purpose of representing them as a people devoted to <hi type="italic">kârath</hi>, or extermination. The origin of this name, which is selected both here and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.16">Eze 25:16</reference> with a play upon the appellative signification, is involved in obscurity; for, as we have already observed at <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sa 30:14</reference>, there is no valid authority for the derivation which is now current, viz., from the island of <hi type="italic">Crete</hi> (see Stark, <hi type="italic">Gaza</hi>, pp. 66 and 99ff.). דּבר יי עליכם forms an independent sentence: The word of the Lord cometh over you. The nature of that word is described in the next sentence: I will destroy thee. The name <hi type="italic">Kena‛an</hi> is used in the more limited sense of Philistia, and is chosen to indicate that Philistia is to share the lot of Canaan, and lose its inhabitants by extermination.
entries.15e57bb41d8a200653f2fa7eaf07478d13e734a5: Zep 2:6-7 <div eID="gen16720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> The tract of land thus depopulated is to be turned into “pastures (<hi type="italic">nevōth</hi>, the construct state plural of <hi type="italic">nâveh</hi>) of the excavation of shepherds,” i.e., where shepherds will make excavations or dig themselves huts under the ground as a protection from the sun. This is the simplest explanation of the variously interpreted <hi type="italic">kerōth</hi> (as an inf. of <hi type="italic">kârâh</hi>, to dig), and can be grammatically sustained. The digging of the shepherds stands for the excavations which they make. Bochart (<hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. i. p. 519, ed. Ros.) has already given this explanation: <hi type="italic">“Caulae s. caulis repletus erit effossionis pastorum,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">caulae a pastoribus effossae in cryptis subterraneis ad vitandum solis aestum.”</hi> On the other hand, the derivation from the noun <hi type="italic">kērâh</hi>, in the sense of cistern, cannot be sustained; and there is no proof of it in the fact that <hi type="italic">kârâh</hi> is applied to the digging of wells. Still less is it possible to maintain the derivation from יכר (Arab. <hi type="italic">wkr</hi>), by which Ewald would support the meaning nests for <hi type="italic">kērōth</hi>, i.e., “the small houses or carts of the shepherds.” And Hitzig’s alteration of the text into כּרת = כּרים, pastures, so as to obtain the tautology “meadows of the pastures,” is perfectly unwarranted. The word <hi type="italic">chebhel</hi> is construed in Zep 2:6 as a feminine <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi>, with a retrospective allusion to <hi type="italic">'erets Pelishtı̄m</hi>; whereas in Zep 2:7 it is construed, as it is everywhere else, as a masculine. Moreover, the noun <hi type="italic">chebhel</hi>, which occurs in this verse without the article, is not the subject; for, if it were, it would at least have had the article. It is rather a predicate, and the subject must be supplied from Zep 2:6 : “The Philistian tract of land by the sea will become a tract of land or possession for the remnant of the house of Judah, the portion of the people of God rescued from the judgment. Upon them, viz., these pastures, will they feed.” The plural עליהם does not stand for the neuter, but is occasioned by a retrospective glance at נות רעים. The subject is, those that are left of the house of Judah. They will there feed their flocks, and lie down in the huts of Ashkelon. For the prophet adds by way of explanation, Jehovah their God will visit them. <hi type="italic">Pâqad</hi>, to visit in a good sense, i.e., to take them under His care, as is almost always the meaning when it is construed with an accusative of the person. It is only in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.6">Psa 59:6</reference> that it is used with an <hi type="italic">acc. pers.</hi> instead of with על, in the sense of to chastise or punish. שׁוּב שׁבוּת as in Hos 6:11 and Amo 9:14. The <hi type="italic">keri</hi> שׁבית has arisen from a misinterpretation. On the fulfilment, see what follows.
entries.d0f823ac4027fb3e7e320974425681a4f5024cc0: Zep 2:8-10 <div eID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16722" type="x-p"/> The judgment upon Joab and Ammon. - Zep 2:8. <hi type="italic">“I have heard the abuse of Moab, and the revilings of the sons of Ammon, who have abused my nation, and boasted against its boundary.</hi> Zep 2:9. <hi type="italic">Therefore, as I live, is the saying of Jehovah of hosts, the God of Israel: Yea, Moab shall become like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrha, an inheritance of nettles and salt-pits, and desert for ever. The remnant of my nation will plunder them, the residue of my nation will inherit them.</hi> Zep 2:10. <hi type="italic">Such to them for their pride, that they have despised and boasted against the nation of Jehovah of hosts.” </hi> The threat now turns from the Philistines in the west to the two tribes to the east, viz., the Moabites and Ammonites, who were descended from Lot, and therefore blood-relations, and who manifested hostility to Israel on every possible occasion. Even in the time of Moses, the Moabitish king Balak sought to destroy Israel by means of Balaam’s curses (Numbers 22), for which the Moabites were threatened with extermination (Num 24:17). In the time of the judges they both attempted to oppress Israel (Jdg 3:12. and Jdg 10:7.; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.5">1Sa 11:1-5</reference> and 2 Samuel 10-12), for which they were severely punished by Saul and David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30-2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:30-31</reference>). The reproach of Moab and the revilings of the Ammonites, which Jehovah had heard, cannot be taken, as Jerome, Rashi, and others suppose, as referring to the hostilities of those tribes towards the Judaeans during the Chaldaean catastrophe; nor restricted, as v. Cölln imagines, to the reproaches heaped upon the ten tribes when they were carried away by the Assyrians, since nothing is know of any such reproaches. The charge refers to the hostile attitude assumed by both tribes at all times towards the nation of God, which they manifested both in word and deed, as often as the latter was brought into trouble and distress. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.26-Jer.48.27">Jer 48:26-27</reference>; and for <hi type="italic">giddēph</hi>, to revile or blaspheme by actions, Num 15:30; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.27">Eze 20:27</reference>; also for the fact itself, the remarks on <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13-Amos.1.2">Amos 1:13-2</reference>:3. יגדּילוּ על גב, they did great things against their (the Israelites') border (the suffix in <hi type="italic">gebhūlâm</hi>, <hi type="italic">their</hi> border, refers to <hi type="italic">‛ammı̄</hi>, my people). This great doing consisted in their proudly violating the boundary of Israel, and endeavouring to seize upon Israelitish territory (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Amo 1:13</reference>). Pride and haughtiness, or high-minded self-exaltation above Israel as the nation of God, is charged against the Moabites and Ammonites by Isaiah and Jeremiah also, as a leading feature in their character (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.11">Isa 25:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29-Jer.48.30">Jer 48:29-30</reference>). Moab and Ammon are to be utterly exterminated in consequence. The threat of punishment is announced in Zep 2:8 as irrevocable by a solemn oath. It shall happen to them as to Sodom and Gomorrha. This simile was rendered a very natural one by the situation of the two lands in the neighbourhood of the Dead Sea. It affirms the utter destruction of the two tribes, as the appositional description shows. Their land is to become the possession of nettles, i.e., a place where nettles grow. <hi type="italic">Mimshâq</hi>, hap leg., from the root <hi type="italic">mâshaq</hi>, which was not used, but from which <hi type="italic">mesheq</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.2">Gen 15:2</reference> is derived. <hi type="italic">Chârūl</hi>: the stinging nettle (see at <reference osisRef="Job.30.7">Job 30:7</reference>), which only flourishes in waste places. <hi type="italic">Mikhrēh melach</hi>: a place of salt-pits, like the southern coast of the Dead Sea, which abounds in rock-salt, and to which there is an allusion in the threat of Moses in Deu 29:22. “A desert for ever:” the emphasis lies upon <hi type="italic">‛ad ‛ōlâm</hi> (for ever) here. The people, however, i.e., the Moabites and Ammonites themselves, will be taken by the people of Jehovah, and be made their possession.
